tldr: A zero-click flaw let plugin authors run code on machines running Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Gemini CLI; two of the four are still unfixed.
Russia opens its first parliamentary election since invading Ukraine, with the only openly anti-war party kept off the ballot.
Saudi Aramco tells European refiners they will get zero contract crude in October after its bypass pipeline was knocked out.
Trump says all 50 states joined his Medicaid most-favored-nation drug pricing model; CMS's own list shows 40 states signed.
Wildcard - Healthcare: Kennedy names eight members to the dormant panel that decides which preventive care insurers must cover for free.
Wildcard - Economics: The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 this week before easing to 4.95%.
Wildcard - International: A vehicle bomb at a mosque beside police offices in Kohat, Pakistan kills at least 21 and wounds about 80.
Wildcard - AI Industry: Crusoe raises $3.9 billion at a $30.9 billion valuation as AI builders shift toward smaller data centers.

items.headline: A zero-click flaw in four major AI coding agents let plugin authors swap in their own code
items.body: Researchers at the security firm AIR disclosed on September 17 a flaw they call Plugin4Shell in Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, GitHub Copilot and Google's Gemini CLI. It breaks SHA pinning, which locks a plugin to one reviewed version: the agent checks out the specified commit but never verifies the code it received matches, so whoever controls the plugin's repository can substitute code that runs with the developer's access and no click. Anthropic patched it in Claude Code 2.1.179 and OpenAI in Codex 0.146.0; Microsoft shipped no patch and no CVE has been assigned.
items.plain: AI coding agents read and write code on a developer's machine, and plugins extend them. The agent is meant to lock each plugin to one exact reviewed version, identified by a fingerprint called a SHA. The researchers found the agents ask for that version but never check they got it. So whoever controls the plugin's repository can quietly hand over different code, which then runs with everything the developer can reach.
items.why: Pinning is the control most enterprises point to when asked how they keep agent plugins safe, and the two agents still exposed are the ones most widely deployed inside large companies.

items.headline: Russia begins its first parliamentary election since the invasion of Ukraine
items.body: Voting for all 450 State Duma seats opened Friday, September 18 and runs through Sunday, the first parliamentary election since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and it includes occupied Ukrainian territory. Authorities barred Yabloko, the only party openly opposing the war, from the ballot; United Russia, the party aligned with President Vladimir Putin, polled near 40%. Russian outlets and rights groups reported roughly 400 Communist Party observers excluded in Voronezh Oblast and public-sector workers in five regions pressed to report voting for United Russia.
items.plain: The State Duma is Russia's lower house of parliament, roughly its House of Representatives. It has not checked the Kremlin for years, so the vote is less about who wins than about what the result is made to look like. The one party that openly opposed the war was kept off the ballot, and voting is running inside occupied parts of Ukraine. Turnout is the number to watch, because it is the one outcome the Kremlin cannot fully script.
items.why: Holding the vote in occupied Ukrainian territory manufactures a paper record of consent there, which Moscow can cite in any future negotiation over those regions.

items.headline: Saudi Aramco tells European refiners they will receive no contract crude in October
items.body: Aramco told European refiners Friday, September 18 that they will receive no crude next month under long-term contracts, according to Bloomberg and Argus Media, which reported the cut applies to all European term buyers. It follows the September 10 drone attack that shut the 1,200-kilometre East-West pipeline, Saudi Arabia's route for moving up to 7 million barrels a day to the Red Sea, damaging three pumping stations and disrupting loadings at Yanbu. Europe had been importing roughly 577,000 barrels a day of Saudi crude; Aramco says it aims to restore full capacity within about six weeks.
items.plain: Most Saudi oil normally leaves through the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. The East-West pipeline exists so oil can cross the country by land and load on the Red Sea side instead, skipping that chokepoint. A drone strike shut it, so the Red Sea port has little to load. Rather than ration everyone, Aramco cut one region entirely: Europe, the farthest away and easiest to supply from elsewhere.
items.why: Cutting a whole region rather than trimming everyone's allocation tells you Aramco expects the outage to last long enough that partial shipments would not have been worth the freight.

items.headline: Trump says every state joined his Medicaid drug pricing model; CMS lists 40 as signed
items.body: Trump announced Friday, September 18 that all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico are joining the GENEROUS model, which ties Medicaid prices for selected brand-name drugs to the lower prices paid in other wealthy countries. CMS's own participant announcement the same day put the signed total at 40 states and Puerto Rico, with the rest having until September 30. Seventeen manufacturers including Pfizer, Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly have agreed to rebate states down to an international benchmark; a White House analysis estimates $64.3 billion in savings over ten years, which KFF notes cannot be independently checked because the agreements are not public.
items.plain: Medicaid is the health program for lower-income Americans, run jointly by states and Washington. Drugmakers charge far less for the same medicine in countries like Germany, where the government negotiates as a single buyer. This model says Medicaid should get that foreign price, with the manufacturer rebating the state the difference. The announced number and the agency's number differ because applying to join and signing are separate steps. And because the contracts are sealed, nobody outside can verify the savings.
items.why: A sealed rebate agreement shifts the savings claim from something auditable to something the administration asserts, which is exactly the arrangement that made earlier drug-pricing deals hard to evaluate.

items.headline: Kennedy restarts the preventive-care panel with eight new members, most of them specialists
items.body: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced on September 17 eight new members of the US Preventive Services Task Force, the volunteer panel whose ratings determine which screenings and preventive drugs insurers must cover with no copay under the Affordable Care Act. Seth Corey, a pediatric hematologist-oncologist, becomes chair, and the roster adds cardiologists, a radiologist and a health economist, filling the panel substantially with specialists rather than primary-care physicians for the first time. It had not met in more than a year after Kennedy canceled a scheduled meeting; the American Medical Association called the slate a “significant departure from the Task Force's traditional membership.”
items.plain: This panel reviews evidence and decides which preventive services actually work, such as at what age a mammogram is worth it. Its top two grades legally force insurers to cover that service with no out-of-pocket cost, so its ratings move money across the insurance market. It was staffed mainly by primary-care doctors, who weigh the harms of over-testing. Filling it with specialists changes who judges the evidence.
items.why: Because a rating change flows straight into what insurers must cover free, the composition of this panel decides out-of-pocket costs for tens of millions of people without any new law being passed.

items.headline: The 10-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since 2007 before easing
items.body: The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield breached 5% on September 14 for the first time in nearly three years, its highest since 2007, before easing to 4.95% Thursday; Bloomberg attributed the selloff to hot inflation, a widening deficit and heavy corporate issuance. The Federal Reserve raised its target range a quarter point on September 16, to 3.75%-4%, its first increase since 2023, with Chair Kevin Warsh saying inflation remains elevated. Stocks ended Friday near flat, the S&P 500 up 0.17% to 7,650.50 and the Dow down 95.40 points, leaving the Dow more than 1.5% lower on the week.
items.plain: The 10-year Treasury yield is what the US government pays to borrow for a decade, and it sets the floor for mortgages and corporate debt. It is not rising because the Fed lifted short-term rates. It is rising because lenders want extra compensation, called a term premium, for holding a long loan while inflation is unsteady and the government keeps borrowing more. Stocks barely moved, which is the surprising part.
items.why: A term premium this large means the government's borrowing costs are now set by bond buyers' doubts rather than by Fed policy, which limits how much the Fed can ease even if it wants to.

items.headline: A vehicle bomb at a mosque next to police offices in northwestern Pakistan kills at least 21
items.body: An attacker rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into a mosque beside a police compound in Kohat, in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, during Friday prayers on September 18, and gunmen then tried to storm the compound, according to the provincial police chief. At least 21 people were killed and about 80 wounded, most of them police officers who had been praying, with early counts ranging from 7 to 27 dead as figures were revised through the day. No group claimed responsibility; officials pointed to the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.
items.plain: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is the Pakistani province along the Afghan border, and Kohat is a garrison town in it. The attackers chose Friday midday prayers because that is when a large number of police are gathered, unarmed and off duty, in a predictable place. The vehicle bomb was meant to breach the compound so gunmen could follow behind it. The Pakistani Taliban is a separate group from the one governing Afghanistan, though it shelters across that border.
items.why: Attacks that kill police in their own compound erode the recruitment and morale that Pakistan's border strategy depends on, which is the point of choosing that target over a civilian one.

items.headline: Crusoe raises $3.9 billion as AI builders shift toward smaller, faster data centers
items.body: Crusoe announced on September 17 the initial close of a $3.9 billion Series F at a $30.9 billion post-money valuation, roughly triple the $10 billion it reached in October 2025, co-led by Atreides Management, Mubadala Capital and Valor Equity Partners with Nvidia and the Qatar Investment Authority participating. Proceeds fund a 352,000-square-foot Colorado factory and a 400,000-square-foot Tulsa plant that opened September 14, both building modular data-center units. CNBC reported separately on September 18 that Anthropic and OpenAI are pursuing smaller data-center deals because large builds are hitting delays across the US.
items.plain: A data center is a building full of computers, and the AI industry's constraint is no longer buying chips but finding somewhere to plug them in. Giant sites need new power lines and substations, which take years and local approval. The alternative is building the data center in pieces in a factory, trucking them to a site and connecting to power that already exists. You give up efficiency and get capacity this year instead of in 2029.
items.why: If modular capacity works, the binding constraint on AI shifts from chip supply, which a few companies control, to electrical interconnection, which thousands of local utilities control.

items.headline: NASA adds $946 million to SpaceX's contract for three more crewed station flights
items.body: NASA announced Friday, September 18 a contract modification worth $946 million adding Crew-15, Crew-16 and Crew-17 to SpaceX's Commercial Crew Transportation Capability contract, bringing SpaceX to 17 missions under it and raising its value to $5.92 billion, with performance running through 2030. SpaceX handles ground processing, launch, on-orbit operations, return and recovery, and keeping its docked capsule available as a lifeboat. Boeing, the program's other provider, has flown one crewed test flight.
items.plain: NASA stopped operating its own crew spacecraft when the shuttle retired in 2011 and now buys seats from companies. The plan was two suppliers, so a problem with one would not strand American astronauts, as happened when NASA bought Russian seats for nearly a decade. Boeing was meant to be the second and is years behind. Booking three more SpaceX flights through 2030 is NASA acknowledging it has one American ride.
items.why: Contracting through 2030 with a single effective provider removes the competitive pressure that was supposed to hold seat prices down for the station's final years.

items.headline: Trump announces a White House ban on three news outlets; their reporters stayed and kept working
items.body: In a Truth Social post at about 3 p.m. Eastern on Friday, September 18, Trump wrote that he was banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House “effective immediately,” calling it “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and adding “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Asked in the Oval Office which stories prompted it, he named none: “It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years, you get sick of it.” CNN reported its journalists remained at the White House and kept covering the administration that afternoon. In Associated Press v. Budowich, decided April 8, 2025, US District Judge Trevor McFadden wrote that “if the Government opens its doors to some journalists … it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints”; a D.C. Circuit panel later stayed that injunction as to the Oval Office and Air Force One as nonpublic forums, leaving it for the East Room.
items.plain: A president cannot strip a news organization's access simply because he dislikes its coverage; a federal judge said so in 2025 when the White House tried to shut out the Associated Press over its refusal to write “Gulf of America.” An appeals court narrowed that, letting the president control the Oval Office and Air Force One while keeping larger rooms open to all credentialed press. So a blanket ban runs into a ruling that already exists.
items.why: The gap between the announcement and the enforcement is the story: a ban that is declared but not carried out produces the confrontation without the legal exposure of actually excluding anyone.
